R: Grup de fete tinere "de măritiș", îmbrăcate în port popular de sărbătoare din Banatul sârbesc. Fotografie de exterior, realizată într-un cadru natural. Fotografia este prinsă de o hârtie de culoare crem. Cartonul are patru tăieturi pentru a fixa coțurile fotografiei. V: Pe verso însemnări manuscrise în creion ( "Banat / Glogon / No. 1 / 274 ASTRA), însemnare manuscrisă cu stiloul "Fete și feciori din Ofcea - Comint. Timiș-Torantal / Cercul Panciova / Foto ing. Th. Filipescu, 10 august 1903", ștampilă "Muzeul "Brukenthal" Sibiu / Nr. 14.364" (cifră scrisă cu cerneală și tăiată).

R: Grup compus din 10 bărbați și 2 femei în port popular de rărbătoare din Banatul sârbesc. Fotografie de exterior, realizată într-o curte, lângă trunchiul unui copac. În fundal se observă o casă. Fotografia este lipită pe un carton de culoare crem, încadrată într-un chenar maro. În partea de jos, însemnare manuscrisă în limba română: "Glogon, în 15 August 1903 / Bărbați și femei din Glogon 8. (Bănat). / Theodor Filipescu, chimist". V: Pe verso însemnări manuscrise în creion ("Banat / Glogon / 374 ASTRA / Col. ASTRA 1905 / Catal. I B 57"), ștampilă "Muzeul "Brukenthal" Sibiu / Nr. 14.303" (cifră scrisă cu cerneală și tăiată); număr inventar MCPR 509.

Fotografie de atelier, cu elemente de recuzită (scaune), reprezentând o pereche în port șvăbesc din Carani, județul Timiș. Hârtia sensibilizată este degradată, iar portretele sunt încadrate într-un medalion oval. Marginile hârtiei prezintă dungi neagre, datorate diferenței de mărime dintre clișeul pe sticlă și hârtia sensibilizată. Retuș manual: ochii bărbatului au fost retusați pe clișeul pe sticlă. Formatul fotografiei este Cabinet Card. Imaginea este lipită pe un carton gros, de culoare crem, degradat. Pe verso însemnare manuscrisă în limba română și germană, indescifrabilă: „Șvabi / Mercydorf / Cărand”. Număr de inventar MCPR 1404.

A carrier walking past baggage (including a rifle and shotgun) laid on the ground during a break in the day's march across Anuakland. Evans-Pritchard notes that he was able to recruit Anuak porters locally in Akobo at the beginning of the two month expedition in March 1935.
A portrait of a seated young man with other youths craning their necks to see the camera, under the shelter of a large canvas tent put up by Evans-Pritchard at Pochala.
Looking along the path ahead through grass savannah a woman carries a gourd vessel on her head, possibly returning from a pool or well nearby.

A homestead with a granary seen from a distance in or near the village of Pochala. Evans-Pritchard estimated the village to have a population of between 500-1000 in 1935, and although being the main settlement of the significant Jowatcuaa clan, it had no headman of its own.
A hut with low eaves within a homestead, with bundles of thatching grass and a pole with objects hanging from it to the right.

Remains of a temporary shelter in domed or beehive style. This type of shelter was known as mogwafatshe and was used by people during the ploughing season for some shade and rest. It was made with bent acacia stems and covered with palm leaves and millet stems.

Woman weaving a storage basket from palm fronds, some dyed brown using bark and root of motsinsila plant. This lady was married to Rra Kesego (meaning Kesego's father) - proper name Mosaroze Moramenwa. Kesego was the mother of Boitlhoko Garebakwena, Christopher Morton's fieldwork assistant. It was in this homestead that Christopher Morton and his wife Catherine stayed whilst carrying out fieldwork in the molapo farming area west of Shorobe.

Mosaroze Moramenwa (also known as Rra Kesego) with his crop of maize in the molapo (seasonal flood plain) at Gweghiri, west of Shorobe. In years past, these fields would have been watered with seasonal flood waters from the Okavango delta, but the gradual lessening of flood waters reaching the area had meant that farmers were relying on seasonal rains only.

At the homestead of Mosaroze Moramenwa (just visible seated in background) at Gweghiri. Left to right: Catherine Mary Morton; unknown (a friend); Boitlhoko Garebakwena, his brother Lekgoana (the grandsons of Mosaroze).

A full length profile portrait of a Bari woman wearing a fringed skirt and arm and neck ornaments, standing in front of a hut entrance, probably at Gondokoro. It seems likely that this image was taken shortly before October 1878 when Buchta reached Lado (Juba) on board S.S. Safia. The hut door is unusual in that it seems to consist of a double door sealed by a large wooden latch, perhaps a chief's residence.

A posed group portrait of three Bari men, probably at Gondokoro. It seems likely that this image was taken shortly before October 1878 when Buchta reached Lado (Juba) on board S.S. Safia. The men have been posed so as to provide front, profile and rear views of Bari male decoration in the same image. Their ornamentation includes feather headdresses and animal fur arm ornaments.

A man wearing a pith helmet and smoking a pipe sitting in a camp chair under the canopy of Evans-Pritchard's tent with a map open on the table in front of him. He is identified as an Austrian Count. Although this might suggest that he could well be the Austro-Hungarian noble László Almásy (1895-1951) who made several trips through Sudan in motor vehicle during this period, it seems that he was in Sudan in 1929, before Evans-Pritchard's Nuer fieldwork. The co-incidence is strong, but there are also differences in appearance, which seems to point to another Austrian Count.

A Lotuko mortuary ritual object, known as nametere. This particular one was made as a reproduction for the Seligmans to record. The nametere is made after death to 'represent' the deceased at a series of funerary ritual dances, after which it is destroyed by those who made it. It is made from a bundle of dry grass wrapped in lengths of bamboo. The Seligmans visited Lotuko country in the early part of 1922, and according to their diary they travelled between these villages by bicycle.

A three-quarter length portrait of a girl wearing a waist cloth and holding a small child on her hip, standing amongst tall maize plants. Around her neck are a variety of bead and metal chain ornaments. She is also wearing a lip and earrings.

A three-quarter length group portrait of four Mandari girls wearing strings of beads around their necks and waist cloths. Girls often wore beads given to them by male admirers, but they did not indicate any age sets or grades amongst the women. They also have scarification patterns on their foreheads after the manner of the nearby Dinka. These did not indicate any initiation procedure however but were done for aesthetically pleasing effect only.

A full length frontal portrait of two Mandari girls with ash decorated faces, wearing checked waist cloths and several strings of neck beads, one a coin pendant. Harvested beans are laid out on the ground in the sun behind them to dry.

A full length portrait of a Mandari woman wearing a checked textile body cloth, with a baby tied to her back. She is also carrying a gourd vessel in a string carrier and on her head a roll of matting. Across the foreground Jean Buxton's shadow wearing a skirt is visible, looking down into her Rolleiflex camera.

A full length portrait of a Mandari woman wearing a leather apron leaning against a fence with a pipe in her mouth [poor photo]. Just visible behind her, propped against the fence, is a bicycle presumably belonging to Jean Buxton.

A young woman with a black ostrich plume in her hair standing on the steps of a raised lomore or courting hut in western Mandari. There were one or more such huts in a homestead belonging to a lineage or extended family, and were places where girls of courting age met young men in the evenings and slept there overnight. A white band painted around the entrance makes them known to others as a lomore.

Album containing photographs and a journal by Capt. Herbert Sutherland Walker, relating to the British military campaign against the Kingdom of Benin in February 1897. The album contains seventy-seven photographic prints by Herbert Sutherland Walker (and/or others); and a handwritten diary by Walker, titled on the first page 'To BENIN & back', with entries dated from 16 January to 16 April 1897. Also in the album are newspaper cuttings, several published illustrations and photographs, and other printed matter. The album has been organised approximately chronologically by the compiler, though not exactly or consistently so, in order to show a narrative of the campaign ('Benin Punitive Expedition').

Full length portrait of the Chief of Baham in front of a house made of bamboo sticks, sitting on a european-like stool. He holds a fly whisk in his right hand and wears a traditional loin cloth as well as a cap. The door behind his back is framed by four richly carved panels, which show human figures and heads (?), as well as two tortoises. A man is standing behind the chief's right shoulder, but inside the house. At the utmost right side of the photograph a pair of hands is visible, holding a small figure (pipe bowl?). See also 1998.112.49.
Entrance to the village of Bansoa. Three boys are standing on a clearance in the foreground, the houses of the village are in the farer background, behind a large tree.

Chief of Bamesing, sitting on a carytid stool in front of a house entrance. The hosue is made of bamboo sticks, the door is framed by richly decorated panels. The panel on top shows a row of human heads, the panels to the left and to the right show two human figures standing on top of each other. The chief holds a flywhisk in his right hand. He wears sandals,a shirt and loincloth as well as a cap. On his right side are three nude woman, one holding a pipe, two holding calabashes. On the left side also stands a nude woman, also holding a pipe, which is decorated with beads.

Chief of Bafoussam, sitting on a stool in front of a royal display cloth. Five mask dancers are standing behind his back, four of them wearing elephant masks, called mbap mteng. The masks are decorated with beads. The chief wears a loincloth as well as a necklace, which forms a snake.

Chief of Basoa, sitting in front of a house. He is dressed in a shirt, showing a geometric design, and wears a matching hat. He also wears european shoes and suspenders. At the right side three young men, one of them holds a fly whisk and a pipe, both objects are decorated with beads. The two other men are dresses in cotton cloth, which also covers their head so that only the faces are revealed. The chief is sitting in front of an entrance, which is framed by richly carved panels, showing human figures and animals.

Half length portrait of a wooden male figure. The figure identified as a commemorative figure for fon Tshakutio de Bazou. The figure wears a necklace as well as a necklace around the hips. The eyes and teeth of the figure are accentuated by white pigment. The figure is also represented with a cap. Both forearms are decorated with several rills, representing bracelets (?). Houses in the background (see also 1998.112.20).

Caryatid stool, the caryatid figure representing an animal (leopard?) with a human face. The rim of the seat is decorated with a geometric design as well as animals, representing lizards (?). The stool stands in front of a house entrance.
Three houses, made of bamboo sticks and clay, surrounding a square place. The house in the centre shows a row of windows, two men are standing in front of this house.

Chief of Batcham, sitting on a stool, his right arm resting on a table. He hold a glas with juice (?) in his right hand, the left hand holds a large pipe. He is dressed in traditinal clothing and wearing a cap. Behind his back three men. Two of the men are wearing traditional clothing, decorated with cowrie shells, the one in the middle is dressed in a european suit and wears a european hat. The man to the left holds a spear in his right hand, the other two men are holding rifles. On the right side of the chief two boys, one directly behind his shoulder, the other one stuck his arm beneath the chief's left arm. This boy also holds an european hat in his left hand. On the left side of the chief, in front of the table, a young girl is leaning against the leg of the chief. In front of her, a young boy is kneeling, holding the pipe bowl. Under the table, there is a caryatid stool (?), representing an animal. On top of the table there is a traditional bottle gourd, decorated with beads, as well as a white european coffee pot. A  traditional textile is used as tablecloth. The group is positioned in a courtyard (?).

This man is definitely not a Luo judging from his personal body adornment. He is probably a Kalenjin as one related note mentions the term 'Lanbua', which could be interpreted as 'Lumbwa', a term used in colonial days for those Kalenjin (such as Kipsigis or Nandi) who lived around Koru and Kipkelion (formerly Fort Tunnel). This is a view of Luo open countryside with gentle hills and open valleys in Ugenya Location, Siaya District. fenced Luo homesteads as can be seen here are set on the gentle hill as the open valleys are farmed. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]

A portrait of a Luo woman (possibly identified as Lenya) from Gangu village, wearing a beadwork headdress (ligisa). The ligisa headdress is open at the top, made of vegetable fibre and sticks, and decorated with glass beads (tigo). She is also smoking tobacco using a long stem (ondhuru) connected to a clay pipebowl (kwesi). Her forehead is also decorated with scarification spots (ngo’l) in horizontal parallel lines (see also 1998.349.113). Behind her is a plantation of a type of sorghum (bel) showing their grain heads and probably ready for harvesting. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]

A portrait of a man seemingly identified as Mboya (or Mbuga) of Uhanya Village in Alego Location. On his head is the cowry shell hat ogut gagi which extends into a cowry shell necklace (tik gagi mar ngut) with glass beads (tigo). He has a finger ring which may be for tapping a smoking pipe (oduong’o) and quite a number of wrist rings (minyonge) on both wrists. His long pole (odunga) is of interest, and was often used when attending a funeral. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]

A composite full-face and profile image of a Bongo funerary figure carving, in the collections of Gordon College, founded in 1902, the precursor of the University of Khartoum. Although noted in his slide list as the funerary figure of a 'Golo "Sheikh"' this composite image (including more of the person holding it) was reproduced in a 1917 article by Seligman as showing a Bongo grave figure. It was said to have been taken from a grave of a chief and from an area along the El Ateesh road from Wau to Tembura, some twelve miles south of Fort Ukanda. [CM 08/01/2007]

A long wooden rain-post (riyak) with maize heads and medicines attached, stuck into the ground under a large nilotic shea-butter tree, Vitellaria paradoxa ssp. nilotica, a slow-growing hardwood fruit tree indigenous to northern Uganda and Southern Sudan. During drought this post was the focus for rain-making rituals involving the sprinkling of durra (Sorghum bicolor) over an assembled crowd by a rain-maker (biriak).

A set of old stone axe-heads and other stone tools, laid out on the ground by Surur the rain-maker for Evans-Pritchard to photograph them (although not touch them) from their home along with his hair clippings in a pot beneath the eaves of his hut. These stones were called landa loma - stones of Loma, a spiritual connection with rain-making. During rain-making Surur would place these stones along with magical medicines in a pot with rock-pool water and sprinkle to the east where the next day was to arrive from.

A stone mound erected over a man's grave (dodo) surmounted by a short pointed stake with a carved pot pierced over it. Around the mound are six carved posts tallying different large animals killed by the deceased, one of which (to the right) is also surmounted by a carved likeness of the man. These carved figures were considered representations of the deceased, put up to honour the individual, but not serving any ritual purpose [very cloudy image].

Two carved wooden funerary figures, one with large horns set on top of a low earth burial mound within a homestead with a large well-thatched crop storage hut raised on piles behind, called a gallotoh by Schweinfurth. Not all Bongo graves were marked with a mound of stones, and such mounds were sometimes erected a number of years later at a mortuary ceremony. These carved figures were considered representations of the deceased, put up to honour the individual, but not serving any ritual purpose. Usually accompanied by tallies of animals killed in hunting, the horns on the figure signify the status of the hunter.

A stone mound erected over a man's grave (dodo) surmounted by a short pointed stake (visible to left) with a carved pot pierced over it. Around the mound are six carved posts tallying different large animals killed by the deceased, two of which are visible in this image, one with a likeness of the deceased carved at the top. These carvings were understood as a means of honouring the dead but did not have any particular ritual meaning.

A long wooden rain-post (riyak) stuck into the ground with a shorter notched post (lingi) for hunting-magic offerings, usually fowl sacrifice. During drought the rain-post was the focus for rain-making rituals involving the sprinkling of durra (Sorghum bicolor) over an assembled crowd by a rain-maker (biriak).

A stone mound near a hut erected over a man's grave (dodo) with three carved posts surmounting the top tallying twenty elephants killed in the hunt by the deceased, placed as a means of honouring him. Around the mound are five more carved posts (some with arrows stuck in them); to the right a likeness of the deceased; to left a forked (horn-shaped) post set up by his son-in-law yet tallying his own buffalo kills. The next is a likeness of the deceased with a tally of two hippo killed, then a forked post tallying six rhino (only tip visible) and lastly a forked post tallying five buffalo with a bowl and matting [cloudy image at centre].

A stone mound near a hut erected over a man's grave (dodo) with three carved posts surmounting the top tallying twenty elephants killed in the hunt by the deceased, placed as a means of honouring him. This type of mask would traditionally depict a beautiful woman and was worn by a male dancer at funerals.

View of a large stone carving at the ancient Maya site of Quirigua located near the banks of the Motagua river in the department of Izabal, Guatemala. The photograph shows the west side of a carved stone stela known by archaeologists as Stela F, as it was first described by Alfred Maudslay in his seminal publication of the Quirigua site in his multi-volume Archaeology (1889–1902): 'This is the most graceful and most elaborately decorated of all the Quirigua stelae. [...] The graceful arrangement of the feather-work on the upper part of this monument is well worthy of note.' More recent scholarship dates the stela (also known as Monument 6) to 9.16.10.0.0, 1 Ahau 3 Zip (Maya calendar), or A.D. 761 in the standard Western (Gregorian) calendar. Considered to be one of the great masterpieces of Mesoamerican sculpture, the monument was created during the later part of the sixty-year reign of K'ak' Tiliw Chan Yopaat and marked the close of an era in the Maya calendar. It was one of a number of stelae and zoomorphs erected at Quirigua as part of a complex building programme which took place at the height of the city-state's power during the Late Classic period, and whose primary aim was to legitimate and reinforce the power of the ruler.

Portrait of a woman, kneeling on a blanket on the ground, polishing the inside of a large clay pot with a smooth pebble.  According to James Stevenson's original note for this photograph (prepared circa 1885), '[a]fter the piece of pottery to be polished is completed and sun-dried, it is taken into the house, a quantity of the same material of which the vessel is made is thoroughly pulverized, and made into a solution, and after all the coarse or gritty substances are removed from it by straining, the solution is applied to the surface of the vessel by means of a rabbit-skin mop.  It is then rubbed with the stone, and the application repeated until the desired smoothness and polish is obtained.  The vessel is again thoroughly sun-dried, and is then ready for the kiln.  Pottery on which it is intended to paint designs is manipulated in the same manner, but no polishing-stone is used after the vessel is decorated.'

Back pack made from woven cucurito palm with bamboo or cane frame; carrying strap made from strips of bark. Open-fronted with bark strips threaded across the opening.

Model of a canoe [A] with an oar and wooden haft [B-C] and a birch bark bailer [D]. Canoe is made from strips of wood and bark with three wooden rods across the top. Chiquitey; small basket for carrying eggs made from Tamshi. Oval opening with reinforcement and band of close weave below; the rest of the basket is woven in an open hexagonal pattern. Long handle of the same material woven through body of basket.

Chiquitey. A small, cylindrical basket with a flat oval base made with tamshi. One length of cane forms the edge and is enclosed by strips. A bark strap has been looped through the wide, hexagonal weave and allows the container to be carried around the forehead, used by both sexes.

Blow gun dart holder of bamboo with gourd stuffed with fluffy plant fibre to hold Wamburusi. Twisted cord strap with small piece of serrated metal for scoring the dart. The cotton like 'feather' to dart is made from palm vein and poisoned with stuff bought from a trader via Iquitos. The bamboo has evidence of woodworm.

Five pairs of ear decorations made of strings of beads terminating in yellow and red toucan feathers; four have four groups of feathers, one has three. All have blue beads, most with red, white or green. One feather from .5 is detached but present.
Humberta. Small bird skin of a purple-vented Euphonia with navy and yellow feathers, stuffed with cotton. Eyes have been removed, and the beak is open.
Dried piece of plant, possibly a root.
Rattle consisting of band of plaited vegetable fibre string with short strings hanging from it along its length. Nutshell hanging from end of each string, with slit cut in bottom to form bell shape.
Goabddá. Divination drum with skin tympanum painted with figures and symbols.

Bag - String handbag, with plaited " root" rings for string to run through
Bowl - Circular wooden bowl carved with human figures hunting deer -like animals on the rim and the flat base.

Tjevet. Wide, man’s kilt of black synthetic fibre with beaded waistband. Front of waistband decorated with band of anthropomorphic faces in orange, green, yellow and red glass beads; small aluminium discs between each face and three rows of beads below in purple, black and green. Two larger anthropomorphic faces wearing ovoid headdresses set at centre thirds. Simple machine stitched hem along kilt bottom and short ties either side of waistband.
Nose flute of bamboo, with incised decoration
Net - Fishing net, ?in course of construction. The hook = " sakurawit" . Bamboo = " tope" . String = " karudo" . String holder = " saunon"

Torana. Door hanging with nine pendant panels, embroidered with Ganesh and decorated with circular mirrors. Rectangular panel of cream coloured woven cotton, bordered with black cloth; embroidered in green, red, blue, brown, yellow and pink with central Ganesh figure, parrots, elephants, geometric and floral motifs; pendant panels are appliquéd with pale green, red, yellow, orange, blue and pink fabrics and decorated with metallic braid and small tassels; five fabric loops at top of the rectangular panel for hanging.
Phremphun. Necklace, religious beads, made of seeds from a tree. May be worn as a necklace as part of Pa-chyu costume.

Ten. Headdress made of feathers from tail of golden pheasant (one bunch red male, one bunch spotted female) joined by cotton band. Bound with black hair of the wild pig. Worn around hat 1993.39. Used by Pa-chyu shaman.

Pyon. Wooden container. Made by Chunar's people and ordered by a shaman on a special day. To make the container, a piece of wood is turned on a hand lathe and cut with a special blade. Used for holding wine to give the ancestors a special drink. Interior has residue of millet wine.
Fagi. Man's traditional white kilt worn for everyday. Made of fine machine-woven cotton. Previously made of hand-woven nettle fibre.
Bell - Old, bronze bell, with hole at top and small, iron loop. From Pinausha Dead House
Necklace - Necklace of seeds, whitish and shiny in appearance
Pair of metal earrings with blue glass beads. Semicircular filigree earring with fringe of curved teardrop shapes; one blue glass bead set into the centre of each side; wire loop for fastening.

Gotol. Pair of black leather boots with thick composite sole. Lined with blue cloth, with a band around the top of the opening; brown leather piping along seams and geometric embroidery at the heel; green and red braided cord around top of sole which consists of layers of leather and cloth; bottom of sole is concave.

Deel, terlig. Man's coat of blue silk, with turquoise cuffs and a green trim to the collar and lapel. the collar stands up and is buttoned at the neck. the proper left side of the coat front overlaps the right, buttoning at the right shoulder. There are subtle patterns in the weave of the coat's fabric.

Circular, broad-brimmed hat with narrow conical projection at centre. Multidirectional plaited strips of cane with sheets of waxed or oiled paper held between; rim reinforced with twisted lengths of cane; central conical projection partially wrapped with strips of cane; row of three motifs painted in black on top of the brim, with two motifs painted in red opposite; row of five circles underneath the brim near the centre.

Sleeveless vest of dark blue cotton. Formed of two panels on the front and back; with a round neck; large armholes that curve inwards; flared body, with slits at both sides of the hem, which is  straight edged on the front and rounded on the back. It has an overlapping panel and closes on the right seam, with a wide ribbon of black silk in two layers, and is lined with a woven pattern of white linked circles on black, fastening at the right shoulder with a 2 annas coin button with shank, displaying queen Victoria on the outward face; and with four more knot and loop fastenings, one broken knot at the neck. Double lined, with light blue interior and black trim around the neck.

Pair of silk shoes with leather soles and upturned toes, decorated with embroidery. Uppers of black silk or satin, lined with undyed cotton and embroidered with floral and geometric patterns in pink, white, green, yellow, orange and blue; decorated with blue to green ribbon and strips and squares of gold-coloured metal; composite soles made from layers of cotton painted white with leather on the bottom; interior of shoe is lined with undyed cotton.
Portrait sculpture in plaster of Heen Hita Wanniya, a Vedda man

Spoon - Wooden spoon used in manufacture of Tibetan paper. Paper pulp made from mashed plant material mixed with water is poured into a wooden frame to dry into sheets. Heavily patinated handle with paper pulp residue throughout.

Weapon - Three small bamboo spikes, "panjis", sharpened at both ends stuck in the ground to impede the progress of enemies. "new caltraps removed from under the fallen leaven in a path leading to the Abor village of Ponging; set againt the coming of any from Rotung where the Abor punitive expedition was" catalogue card.; Good; Whole.

Sleeveless coat or waistcoat made from a takin (goat) hide. Square back panel with tail protruding at the base; front panels with notch at the opening and a small rectangular panel at the back of the neck; panels sewn together with cotton thread; large metal safety pin at front, possibly originally used as a fastening. Several contemporary repairs.
Rectangular piece of cloth of woven pland 'pud' fibres, made up of two pieces sewn together, natural or light brown in colour with paired wefts.
Canework comb. Non-ceremonial, and worn by ordinary tribesmen.

Zastera. Woman's apron. The apron is white with embroidered decorations of floral and heart-shaped motifs in red, green, orange, pink, blue, and purple. The top half is bordered by pink ribbons and a red panel with blue ribbons arranged in a diamond pattern. The bottom half is pleated. There is a border with red embroidered designs and a pink trim.

Skladaná sukna. Purple skirt. Pleated with three bands of black near the bottom. The top is finished with green fabric on one side and blue on the other. There are black strings for tying and a safety pin.
A length of cloth woven with floral designs and other patterns in red and yellow.
Beige table cloth embroidered with cross stitch patterns in beige, blue, and white in Hardanger-style.
A piece of cloth with embroidered patterns in red, blue, and yellow. Possibly a piece of an unfinished cap.
One miniature parka for a doll, made of alternating white and brown fur with white fur lining the opening. The sleeves are very short with some purple fabric appliqué across the shoulders.
Lasso - Reindeer suede lasso made from a four-stranded plait, with antler fastening lug.
Pin made of blackthorn wood, trimmed and fried in fat, made by Leviathon Pickett. One terminal tapers to a point, the other is flat.

Tamata. Votive offering. Stylised representation of a standing child, hand modelled in olive green wax. Its right hand rests on its left hip and its left hand is placed on its abdomen. A loop of string protrudes from the top of its head suggesting a point of suspension. The eyes are black-eyed beans pushed into the wax. The right forearm is damaged, wax has cracked and fallen away.

Tamata. Votive offering. Stylised representation of head and neck, hand modelled in green wax. The hair is shoulder length and there is a pink patch of colour at the back of the head. The eyes appear to have been gauged out. A loop of string protrudes from the top of its head, suggesting a point of suspension.

Tamata. Votive offering. A heart shape, stamped on thin, silver sheet to produce a slightly raised design. Incised detail around outline. There is a semicircular tab and hole at the top for the attachment of a pin.
Tamata. Votive offering. Rectangular piece of sheet silver metal with chased depiction of a male bust wearing a suit. Hole at top centre, for the attachment of a pin.

Sacred bamboo flute covered for most of its length, except for mouth-hole, with plaited cane sleeves, coloured blackish red. Black cassowary feathers attached to the coiled cane work flange at mid-length.

Small, almost square bilum bag, netted from thick twine in double figure of 8 rows. Dark brown coloured loop stitching attaches separately netted rim band. Netted carrying strap crosses over from top corners. 8 rows of pale blue, brown and dark brown rectangles contrast with natural/pale brown background. A few brown rectangles occur between the other rows, but the overall appearance is of a rough check design. Made by Tshuosh, in neighbourhood of Berui village. Original accession notes: " Pattern worked in dyed string. Carried suspended from the head by women. Bought from Tshuosh by Iatmul." Good.

Full-length male hook figure on 2-pronged hook base. Ovoid head with fine black on white face painting. Conus shell eye inlay. Initiatory marks on breasts and navel are represented in white paint which also decorated the tip of the penis and the knees.
Pair of false breasts made of conical gourd halves worn by men on ceremonial occasions. eg. Naven and in certain initiatory ceremonies, in which the initiators are spoken of as NYAME ("Mothers")

Narrow openwork wooden board carved with distinct face and 2 curved hook prongs in each of 2 windows near base. Toothed top with piereced point as central boss and pierced semioval ' ears' at corners. Rough overcoiled loop attached through piercings. Slight curve design on the forehead. Hook eyes. Long nose with pierced bird design in profile with a knobbed beak ridge. Nose reaches to ' chest' . Cheek marks semiovoid, lying at base of cheek area. Crescent mouth with two globular curls at each side, followed by triangular tips. Main body panel carved with 2 bird's in centre whose beaks interlock round rod. Pierced lobefaces cover rest of body panel. Base carved with scroll or spiral design. Baseline flat except for rounded corners and point projecting in centre. Faint remains of white (particularly on face background and on the uppermost birds), red and black pigments. No face at rear. An old crack lies across lower half, now glued. Rough cane bindings which formerly held pieces together still in place. Colours faded. Original accession notes: " Large openwork carving representing the face of the sago-beetle (cf. 1930.341)." Fair
Beater for gong. Stick with circular cross-section and small conical stepped butt. Tip expanded and rounded with face carved on one side. No colouring, carving very shallow.

Half-length wooden figure with circular base. Triangular cap on top of head, prominent forehead line, small ovoid eyes, raised cheek areas, large club nose and mouth with rod teeth spread wide above projecting chin. Plaited fibre is knotted around neck and through nose. Shoulder area and breasts pointed. Arms flexed outwards at elbows, rejoining body, handless, at hip rim. A hole is pierced through the face sideways which maybe the vagina on cheek referred to in the accession note. Below hip line a vulva inside a pubic trianble is discernable. Prominant on the belly is an oval rim, representing labia, above the ovoid navel knob. Near base, centre rear, an anus hole is carved. Light toothed carving on shoulders and mouth. Piercing through shoulders on back (for hanging up?). Faint touches of white paint, projecting surfaces have become very smooth through much handling. Original accession notes: " Wooden figure ? female with vagina on cheek. ' Belong Blas in Tambaran', blas = flute, so this is a flute ornament ?" Fair

Kait Nambu. Ovoid pith head attached to centre of buttock ornament 1935.9. Raised forehead cap, painted black. Oval eye cavities in black hook eyes. Double pierced semiovoid ear lugs with slight remains of fibre in one piercing. Squashed club nose, broad curved lips. Raised cheeks. Rear of head domed at top, with lipped cavity for lower half. Face painted with black curvilinear design against white. Badly chipped with pieces missing, paint worn.

Dance waist ornament used by by Mwai and impersonators of Wagan. A curved rod frame is used to suspend ornaments and at present this includes the enemy portrait head (1935.10A) and long pith toggles on the spiked halo frame.

Large barkcloth mask with red and black painted designs and fibrous leaf tassels at bottom, used in Baining spirit night dance.  The spirit represents a type of leaf “rengit”, also used to wrap food for ceremonies.
Carinated jug with short spout and two handles. Decorated with panels of dark glaze and dark pink patterns; Dar, Thebana and Jerida (the horse, the fly and the palm leaf).
A sister basket, circular, plaitwork basket, with "bossed" faces and loop handle. It is decorated with a pattern in a darker colour
Pot of burnished black ware. Upright rim and tall neck, globular protrusion then cylindrical body and flat base. Directed with linear patterns. Small chips to base.

Small pot of burnished red ware. Everted rim, short neck and narrow mouth, rounded body tapering to a flat base. Decorated above the shoulder and below the neck with linear markings, incised with a fine pointed stick. Bound by horizontal lines are rows of short vertical lines.

Bow, made from polished red coloured wood with a circular cross section. The bow is decorated at each end with monkey tail, one being bound at the end with an iron strip. Most of the hair has come away from the tail. The bow string is made from bamboo, knotted around both ends. The bow string has broken away from the knot on one side.

Four arrows with wooden shafts and leaf fletchings. [A] has a socketed leaf shaped blade with barbed shoulders and is bound on the shaft with coiled metal. [B] has a socketed, rounded blade and is bound near the fletching with coiled metal. [C] has a socketed blade with barbed shoulders; socket is wrapped with a strip of metal. [D] has no head, the terminal is tapered to a point.

Tobacco pipe. Bowl of dark brown pottery coated in black slip. Cylindrical pottery stem with sharp elbow and flaring bowl. A shallow groove runs around the top of the stem and the join between bowl and pottery stem. Wooden stem tapers evenly with a cylindrical socket inserted into the pottery bowl.

Woven cotton cloth, white background with red and orange stripes down long edges, both short edges with two stripes of black then stitched rectangular shapes followed by a series of red lines with lines of black geometric patterns including zigzags and diamond shapes.
A rectangular cloth made from two panels of cream cotton sewn together. The cotton is woven with red and grey stripes, and embroidered with a diamond pattern in dark blue.

Male funerary ornament. Two small disc ornaments, made of plant fibre, possibly cane, wrapped in dark blue cotton threads, connected by long strands of purple wool, wrapped in pink cotton thread at disc attachment point. Discs embellished with bronze coloured beads, probably glass.

Circular inner headband covered in red felt and wrapped in thin metal. Outer decorated with tufts of red, green and yellow felt with small metal fibres from which hang numerous rectangular pendants, some tied into thin metal on inner band.

Pennanular gilded brass armlet. Made from sheet metal, rolled over at the edges to create a hollow tubular shape; protruding pyramidal forms around the outer surface; gilded on the outer surface. One of four armlets, 1944.22.6.13-16.
Meithei polo bridle. Iron snaffle bit, headstall covered in red cloth, decorated with blue, red and white braid at edges, and with white "pompoms". Red cord rein.
Necklace comprising strings of blue, yellow and white beads on red thread. Worn by young men and women.
Bracelet  - Four plain bracelets of solid brass. Worn in sets of seven on either arm by Oraon women
Nambri. Ornament for the lobe of the ear. Worn by women.
Tora. Bangle. Worn on the wrist by women.
Toy  - Spinning top with cord and toggle, made of apple wood.

Kwanget-ap-lakok. Simple bow made from wood with circular cross-section tapering towards either end. Paler areas at each end, likely from the attachments for the missing string. Said to be a boy's bow.
A knife or fleam. The blade is thin with a curved cutting edge, it is set into a wooden stick and secured with hide binding. Used for the blood letting of oxen.

Simple bow with slight recurve. Wooden bow with circular cross-section tapering towards either end; iron wound around one end, with a leather strip below; wide band of leather around bow, possibly a grip. Lighter area of wood indicating missing leather strip.

Quiver (.1) made from hollow bamboo covered in leather with a stitched leather lid attached via a long narrow shoulder strap. (.2-20) poisoned arrows all with feather fletchings, some of which are now missing but the binding remains. The heads are metal, 14 leaf shape, three arrow and two spike. The fire stick (.21) is made from a long narrow branch and is charred at both ends.

Kikoi, a man's wrap around skirt. Made of two woven equal width strips stitched together to form a rectangular skirt of horizontal purple, green, red, blue and pink stripes with plaited fringe at either end.

Purse decorated with coloured glass beads, with a leather lining, a small internal pocket, a hinged opening framed with metal, and a hinged metal clasp. Both sides have the same design, consisting of Greek script in blue, and a floral motif in green, yellow and blue, all on a white background. The top and base have green, blue and red stripes.
A pair of black leather shoes with pointed toes and block heels. There are metal segments attached to the soles; the inside is line with floral fabric.

Lapudzi. Pair of woollen socks knitted with a ribbed cuff in stripes of navy, maroon, white, green, purple and pink with bands of stranded decoration. Striped black and white fabric reinforces the heels.

Kameushu. A long man’s shirt made from cotton with a white, grey and blue check pattern, with zig-zag details. The shirt has long sleeves, a short collar, waist band, and a full pleated skirt section. The shirt is fastened down the front with four shell buttons, and there is pleating either side of the buttons; the cuffs are also fastened with shell buttons. The proper right armpit appears to have been repaired with black stitching.
A pair of men’s white linen drawers, with short legs and a draw string waistband.
A long, rectangular sash of black wool, with tassels along the two short edges.
Horn of elephant ivory covered with hide, with leather cover for mouth. Decorated with iron and copper chains from which are suspended small folded metal ornaments.

Spear, with small, leaf-shaped, socketed iron blade with central midrib. One side of the blade is slightly dented. Long shaft tapers towards the end. The surface of the shaft is slightly uneven due to the natural grain of the wood.
Helmet, the foundation is made of hair and fibre covered with multiple bronze plates. The top is decorated with circular bronze discs, many of which are missing.
Dance rattle. Consists of a leather strap knotted closed at one point; multiple goat or antelope hooves are attached to the strap with twisted fibre sting. Worn by men on the arm or leg.
Small tortoise shell bell. There is evidence of wear across the top of the shell, the head opening and one at side at the tail end.
Ornament to be worn in the hair. Circular disc of leather with a spiral of glass beads stitched to it; translucent red, striped blue and white, and opaque white beads.
Ornament to be worn in the hair. Circular disc of leather with a spiral of glass beads stitched to it; translucent red and opaque white beads.

Cup, made of half a gourd and used by women for drinking. The gourd is decorated with rings of geometric patterns, filled with black pigment. There is a small perforation at the stem of the gourd, through which a small loop of hide.
Bowl for milk, used by royalty. Circular wooden bowl with flattened base and everted rim; stained dark red to brown.

Earthenware pot with a rounded body, everted rim and three cylindrical legs, covered in a red pigment. There are blackened areas across the pot. The rim is damaged and one leg is detached but present.

A milk pot, globular in shape with a narrow, everted rim and rounded base. The outer body of the vessel has a reflective, dark grey glaze; likely derived from graphite. On the inside vertical lines radiate from the centre of the base. A section of the body and rim has been reconstructed from sherds.

Large-bowled, black burnished clay pipe with a wooden stem. The bowl is globular, with a very narrow everted rim, and is decorated just below the rim with delicately incised zigzag shading. The stem-piece is bound near the top with stripes of fine copper wire.  The interior of the bowl is covered with rough corrugation.
